analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve presidential wars, major arms sales, and extended national emergencies.
analysis.headline: The National Security Powers Act, introduced by a Democrat, a Republican, and an independent, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced presidents to get Congress's approval before sending U.S. forces into hostilities, before finalizing large arms sales to most countries, and before keeping a declared national emergency in place beyond 30 days. It also would have repealed the decades-old authorizations for the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and the 1957 Middle East force authorization, replacing the existing War Powers framework with a new one. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain a check on a president's ability to take the country into war, sell weapons abroad, and run the government under endless declared emergencies. Taxpayers would see the estimated costs of any military operation laid out to Congress, and unauthorized military operations would lose their funding automatically. Members of Congress regain the decision power the Constitution assigns them over war, weapons sales, and emergencies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Citizens seeking checks on presidential war powers

how_it_helps.text: Sunsets, 180 days after enactment, the 2001 and 2002 war authorizations and the 1957 Middle East authorization that presidents have relied on for decades of military operations, so old votes can no longer justify new wars.

Requires the president to submit a detailed hostilities report and obtain a specific congressional authorization before introducing U.S. forces into hostilities, with forces required to withdraw within 20 to 30 days if Congress does not approve, and cuts off funding for any unauthorized operation.

Requires an affirmative act of Congress before major arms sales, exports, leases, or loans above set dollar thresholds can go through — for example, firearms deals of $1 million or more and aircraft or munitions deals of $14 million or more — with a fast-track prohibition option only for NATO members and close allies like Japan, South Korea, Israel, Australia, New Zealand, and Taiwan.

Caps any declared national emergency at 30 days unless Congress enacts a joint resolution approving it, imposes an absolute 5-year limit on any emergency, and requires public, detailed reporting on what emergency powers are being used and what money is being moved.
Blocks presidents from inferring war authority from appropriations bills, treaties, or UN resolutions unless Congress passes legislation explicitly authorizing the use of force.

analysis.who_pays: The presidency loses unilateral control over war, arms sales, and emergency powers. Defense contractors and U.S. arms-export agencies lose the fast, largely automatic approval process for big foreign weapons deals, since each major sale would now need a vote of Congress. Foreign governments outside the allied exemption list — for example Middle Eastern buyers — would face slower, more uncertain access to U.S. weapons. In emergencies, the executive branch would lose its special powers after 30 days unless Congress votes to extend them.
analysis.who_pays_short: The presidency and arms-exporting defense contractors

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the 2001 and 2002 use-of-force authorizations 180 days after passage without replacing them, which could cut off the legal authority for ongoing counterterrorism operations against groups like al-Qaeda and its affiliates mid-conflict.
It repeals the War Powers Resolution outright rather than reforming it, removing the existing notification and withdrawal framework that has governed war-powers disputes since 1973.

The 30-day emergency limit and the new requirement that Congress affirmatively approve emergencies could let a hostile or gridlocked Congress block legitimate emergency measures, including economic sanctions authorities under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, which the bill amends.

Requiring a full act of Congress for each major arms sale could slow or block deals that support allied defense needs and U.S. defense-industrial jobs, even for sales that enjoy broad support, because a single chamber can withhold approval.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would restore a genuine check on unilateral presidential war-making, weapons dealing, and emergency rule — powers that presidents of both parties have stretched for decades. But its strongest provisions are blunt: sunsetting existing force authorizations without replacements could disrupt live counterterrorism operations, and the 30-day emergency clock could be used to obstruct legitimate responses. A more carefully tailored version might have attracted broader support; this version was designed to make a constitutional point as much as to become law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Chris Murphy introduced the bill on July 20, 2021 together with Sen. Mike Lee, a conservative Republican, and Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent — an unusual left-right coalition against executive war powers.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it.
The committee held no hearing or markup, and the full Senate never considered the bill before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Presidents keep their unilateral authority over war, national emergencies, and arms sales, and defense contractors keep the existing arms-sale approval process, in which Congress can only object rather than approve.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The executive branch and defense contractors

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Joined Murphy in introducing the bill, lending conservative support to war-powers limits.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined Murphy in introducing the bill.

against.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, which received no committee action after referral and died there.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship crossed party lines — one Democrat, one Republican, and one independent put it forward — but it never reached a vote, so no party split on passage was ever recorded.

industries.note: Major foreign arms sales would need an affirmative vote of Congress instead of surviving by default, and emergency-sale waivers would be narrowed and time-limited. This slows and shrinks the pipeline of weapons deals that make up a large share of industry revenue.

Presidents would lose the ability to start or continue military operations, renew decades-old emergency declarations, and finalize big weapons transfers without Congress. Because the White House is not a commercial industry, its stake is institutional power rather than revenue.

industries.industry: Foreign arms buyers outside the allied exemption list
industries.note: Governments such as Middle Eastern buyers would lose the near-automatic access to U.S. weapons above the bill's thresholds, since Congress would have to authorize each deal. NATO members and close allies like Japan, Israel, and Australia keep a faster track.
